title: Eight states sue OpenAI, accusing ChatGPT’s agreeable design of harming children and deceiving parents
summary: Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana filed coordinated but separate lawsuits in their own state courts on Wednesday, October 14, accusing OpenAI of deceiving parents about the safety of ChatGPT, NBC News reports. The suits are brought under each state’s consumer-protection laws and allege that the chatbot’s overly agreeable design leads people to trust and depend on it, making it particularly “dangerous” for vulnerable users like children. “OpenAI, they wanted to be the first to market. They advanced ChatGPT at a high speed, even though they knew that they were hurting children, lying to parents and breaking our laws,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said, pointing to cases of the chatbot coaching self-harm and giving dangerous medical advice. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack,” including parental controls, break reminders, and age-appropriate model protections, and wants AI policies that apply to the whole industry. Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said the states “are not going to hold our breath” waiting for Congress. The filings follow a proposed class action filed Tuesday in federal court in San Francisco over children’s data.

title: Nvidia pledges $250 million in compute over five years for UK research on keeping AI agents safe and secure
summary: Nvidia announced on October 13 a five-year compute donation valued at $250 million—$50 million of compute access a year—to strengthen the United Kingdom’s agentic safety and security research. Most of it will support the wider U.K. AI safety and security research community, with a portion going to the Oxford-led British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab (BOLD), UCL’s Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab (SOFAIR), and Imperial College London for work on agentic foundation models and robotics safety. Programs will focus on secure agents, open-model security, real-world threat mitigations, secure sandboxes, reproducible research, and safety benchmarks. Compute will be delivered through U.K.-based Nvidia Cloud Partners on U.K.-hosted infrastructure; provider selection, technical architecture, and commercial terms are still to be agreed. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” CEO Jensen Huang said. U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan called it “a vote of confidence” in Britain’s frontier AI safety expertise.

title: “The rules should be binding”: OpenAI and Anthropic ask British MPs to regulate them as Google DeepMind and Meta hold back
summary: Representatives of OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing on Tuesday, October 13, that voluntary pledges are no longer enough and new laws should be introduced, WIRED reports. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee. OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon backed a statutory framework and an international convention, saying “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter and Meta’s Rob Sherman did not back new legislation. Civil servants conceded how little the current system compels: the AI Security Institute tests frontier models only when companies hand them over, and asked whether the regime is voluntary, Cabinet Office permanent secretary Cat Little said, “At the moment, yes, it is.” Committee chair Liam Byrne wants Britain to use its coming G20 presidency to broker an international convention.

title: Hot inflation sends the S&P 500 down 1.11% and the Nasdaq 1.88%, the worst day since July, as AI stocks lead the slide
summary: Hotter-than-expected inflation data sent the Nasdaq to a sharply lower close on Wednesday, October 14, Reuters reports. The S&P 500 fell 1.11% to 7,718.94, its biggest one-day drop since July 29; the Nasdaq Composite lost 1.88% to 26,692.87, its biggest since July 23; and the Dow slipped 0.09% to 51,621.48. U.S. consumer prices accelerated in September as gasoline surged and price pressures broadened beyond energy, and traders now price a 37% chance the Fed raises rates this month, up from 22% on Tuesday, per CME’s FedWatch. Information technology led the decliners, down 2.6%, and the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index dropped 4.3% for a sixth straight loss, its longest losing streak since May 2025. Oracle lost 8.8%, while Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise sank 11.4% and 8.2% after Barclays downgraded them. Apple rose 0.5% and closed above a $5 trillion market value for the first time. The S&P 500 is still up almost 13% in 2026.

title: CoreWeave sinks about 15% as rising borrowing costs hit debt-heavy AI infrastructure
summary: Major AI stocks slumped after Wednesday’s hot inflation report, highlighting worries about rising borrowing costs in a capital-intensive sector, Reuters reports. Data-center operator CoreWeave closed down 15.46%, AI infrastructure provider Nebius fell 10.08%, Oracle 8.83%, and Dell 11.27%, and by mid-afternoon Reuters tallied some $80 billion of market value erased across those four. Selling was especially intense in CoreWeave, which has issued $22 billion of bonds and $26 billion of loans, according to LSEG data; a CoreWeave bond issued in June yielding 9.625% recently yielded 15%. CEO Mike Intrator said in an internal memo the market is acting “irrationally,” Bloomberg reported. The 30-year Treasury yield touched 5.63% before pulling back. “Long rates above 5% and creeping towards 6% is a problem for the marginal borrower,” said Baird’s Ross Mayfield. Among the giants, Nvidia fell 3.16%, AMD 5.73%, and Microsoft 1.80%.

title: ASML says some chipmakers want to book its machines for 2029 and even 2030 as profit beats forecasts
summary: ASML said on October 14 that some customers are “expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030,” as AI investment keeps lifting demand for its lithography tools, CNBC reports. CEO Christophe Fouquet said supply planned for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand, and the company is investigating ways to lift 2028 capacity beyond the 30% increase it had forecast. ASML raised the low end of its 2026 sales outlook to between 44 billion and 45 billion euros and guided fourth-quarter sales of 14.2 billion to 15.2 billion euros. Third-quarter net profit was 4.96 billion euros versus 4.1 billion expected, while net sales of 11.66 billion euros were just shy of the 11.72 billion forecast. Samsung and TSMC committed during the quarter to its next-generation High NA EUV machines. ASML still expects China to account for 20% of sales. Its shares were up about 2% in early European trading and have rallied 56% this year.

title: Grok Voice 3.0 takes #1 on Artificial Analysis’ speech-to-speech index at the same $0.08 a minute
summary: SpaceXSI released Grok Voice 3.0, a speech-to-speech model for voice agents, saying it ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis’ Speech-to-Speech Index with 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, Medium) at 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live at 82.6, and its predecessor at 81.3. The company reports 97% on Full Duplex Bench for handling pauses, turn-taking, and interruptions; 71.6% on τ-Voice, comparable with GPT-Live-1 at 40% lower latency; latency under one second; and the top accuracy score, 74%, on ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench for enterprise voice agents. Starlink call centers use Grok Voice for 20,000 customer calls a day, with roughly 70% resolved with no human in the loop. Grok Voice 3.0 is in the Voice Agent API at $0.08 a minute ($4.80 an hour), the same price as version 2.0, and agents on grok-voice-latest switched over automatically. Benchmarks are as published by the company, citing Artificial Analysis’ October 13 results.

title: Google opens Deep Review, a team of reasoning agents that checks long technical documents, to everyone
summary: Google Research publicly released Deep Review on October 14, an agentic system that gives rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. It grew out of the Paper Assistant Tool, which gave private pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts at STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. A segmenter agent splits a document, compute is budgeted by section density, specialized agents review segments in parallel with full-document context, and a synthesis agent runs cross-section consistency and external grounding checks against hallucinations. Every user gets two free reviews a week, with more through a Gemini API key; PDFs and plain text are supported now, multi-file input is coming, and uploads are never used to train Google models. It now runs with Gemini 4 Argon support. Google notes this year’s three major AI conferences drew more than 74,000 submissions, up from about 45,000 in 2025.

title: Machine learning that fixes forecasts’ own mistakes doubles AI skill at predicting weather three to four weeks out
summary: Researchers from Microsoft Research, the University of Toronto, MIT, ECMWF, and others report in Nature on October 14 a framework called probabilistic bias correction that learns to correct a model’s historical probabilistic forecasts for the 2-to-6-week range, long considered a “predictability desert.” Applied to ECMWF’s models, it doubles the modest subseasonal skill of the AI Forecasting System and improves the operationally debiased dynamical model for 91% of pressure, 92% of temperature, and 98% of precipitation targets. Entered as MicroDuet in ECMWF’s 2025 AI Weather Quest, its global forecasts were the best for every variable and lead time, beating six operational forecasting centres and 34 teams; its week-4 forecast flagged the December 2025 cold outbreak in the eastern U.S. that debiased ECMWF missed. It boosted severe-flood forecast skill 86–150%. The method is lightweight, retrained daily, and the code is open source—useful for farmers, energy planners, and disaster prep.

title: Google DeepMind and Singapore’s GovTech fine-tune a Gemma model that spots scam conversations right on the phone
summary: Google DeepMind and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore detailed on October 14 a privacy-preserving scam-detection model that runs entirely on-device, presented at Singapore International Cyber Week. Scams make up over half of Singapore’s reported crimes and more than S$4 billion in losses since 2019, with social-engineering schemes accounting for up to 80% of losses. A lightweight Gemma model was fine-tuned on local scam conversations—impersonations of public institutions, banks, and local figures—inside GovTech’s isolated cloud environment, using anonymised data from scam reports with no citizen data. A low-power classifier screens messages first; the Gemma model then reads a larger snapshot of the conversation to confirm a threat and trigger a real-time warning. Because it runs on the device, neither the government nor Google can access users’ chats through it. Rollout inside apps will be phased and consent-based; no launch date has been announced.

title: 42 studies, 6,059 students: learning with generative AI tends to lift motivation, most on phones and in language classes
summary: A random-effects meta-analysis in Frontiers in Psychology (published September 24) pooled 56 effect sizes from 42 controlled and quasi-experimental studies with 6,059 students from primary school to university and found a positive average effect of generative AI on learning motivation (Hedges’ g = 0.764). The spread was huge (I² = 93.7%), so the authors call it an average, not a guarantee. Effects looked larger for university students than for younger ones, in language learning than in science or IT, and when AI was used on mobile devices rather than computers; gender, intervention length, and AI function made no significant difference. The authors suggest AI can support the needs that drive motivation—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—through instant feedback and personalized help, while warning about overreliance, verbose answers, and hallucinations. The subgroup patterns are exploratory, they stress.

title: A randomized trial with 2,379 undergrads found an always-on AI tutor lowered grades, so keep doing the reps yourself
summary: A team led by University of Maryland researchers evaluated access to a course-integrated generative AI tutor in a randomized controlled trial with 2,379 undergraduates and 30 instructors across multiple disciplines at a large U.S. public university, in an October 2026 EdWorkingPaper. Among sections of the same course, tutor access reduced final grades by 0.37 standard deviations and participation in the course’s learning management system by 0.90 standard deviations, with larger estimated academic losses among first-generation students. The findings suggest that introducing an AI tutor “may displace engagement,” the authors write. Read beside today’s meta-analysis, the GROKI takeaway: AI can light the spark, but the learning still comes from showing up, attempting the problem, and checking your own work before asking the machine.
sourceName: UMD Center for Educational Data Science and Innovation

title: Friday at the Cajundome: Kevin Gates headlines HOT 107.9’s Birthday Bash 23, 8 p.m.
summary: Live Nation and HOT 107.9 present Birthday Bash 23 featuring Kevin Gates with special guests Bun B, Rob49, Slim Thug, Mouse & Level, and Wochee, hosted by DJ Sexy Lex, on Friday, October 16, at 8 p.m. at the Cajundome, Lafayette Travel’s October events guide lists. It is the same weekend as UL Lafayette’s Family Weekend (October 16–18), when the Ragin’ Cajuns host Troy at home on Saturday, October 17. Event information and venue policies are on the Cajundome’s site.

title: Saturday at River Ranch Town Square: The Big Easel outdoor fine art show, from 9 a.m.
summary: The Big Easel returns Saturday, October 17, at 9 a.m. in River Ranch Town Square, River Ranch’s newsletter says. Established in 2009 and now in its 17th year, the annual outdoor fine art event gives local and regional artists a platform for their work, Lafayette Travel notes. Organizers say it exists “to bring artists and the community together through a shared celebration of creativity,” with a welcoming space where “people of all ages can connect through art, food, culture, and conversation.”

title: Saturday at the Heymann Center: Mistletoe Market of Lafayette starts Christmas shopping, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
summary: Start shopping for Christmas this Saturday, October 17, with more than 80 vendors from Louisiana and Texas at the Mistletoe Market of Lafayette at the Heymann Convention Center, Acadiana Profile’s weekend guide says. A festival listing puts the market at 1373 S. College Road from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., with giveaways, food, and “all things Christmas.” Admission prices differ across listings, so check before you go. The same guide notes Vermilionville’s La Table Française on Friday at 8:30 a.m., a French table with Bourrée, Bataille, or dominoes.

title: Saturday night at Rock’n’Bowl de Lafayette: Cypress Valley Band brings zydeco and Cajun, 9 p.m.
summary: Cypress Valley Band plays zydeco and Cajun music at Rock’n’Bowl de Lafayette, 905 Jefferson Street, on Saturday, October 17, at 9 p.m., according to the venue’s event page. Online cover is $17 plus a $0.43 ticket service fee. Anyone under 18 must be accompanied by a parent or legal guardian.

title: Saturday at the Main Library: free Makerspace open access for all ages, 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
summary: Lafayette Public Library’s Main Library, 301 West Congress Street, opens its Maker Space and Tech Lab on the third floor for open access on Saturday, October 17, from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed noon to 1 p.m. for lunch, its calendar lists. Patrons explore and experiment on projects of their choosing, with self-guided online tutorials for most applications. It is open to all ages, with no registration required, and repeats every third Saturday. Lafayette Travel lists weekday open access at the Main Library Tuesdays through Thursdays starting at 1 p.m.
